food.text: By 1914, intensive farming of sugar and other root crops had made Germany the most efficient agricultural producer in Europe. Farmers abandoned traditional, inefficient practices in favor of artificial fertilizers and mechanical tools.

From 1840 to 1841, Munich had about 83,000 citizens, and 76,979 calves were slaughtered there, statistically approximately one calf per citizen. About 20,000 cows were slaughtered as well. Space in town was so short that most people could only keep two or so small animals in ground floor crates at the rear of their houses, so calves nearing maturity had to be slaughtered or sold out of town.
Colonial goods shops spread in Germany only in the 19th and early 20th centuries. They brought luxury goods like cocoa, coconuts, rare exotic spices, coffee and non-herbal tea to a wider audience.

Munich's city dwellers ate more meat than rural Bavarians, because more people in the city could afford beef. On festival days, roast veal was preferred, and bratwursts of beef were especially popular.

In the 19th century, the vegetables most Bavarians usually ate were Sauerkraut and beets. Potatoes were also accepted as part of Bavarian cuisine, but they could still not replace the popularity of Dampfnudel.

French-influenced dishes such as Ragouts, Fricassee and Böfflamott, a larded and marinated beef, were mostly reserved for the nobility in Bavaria. They were later adopted into the cuisine of ordinary people.

The Bavarian dukes, especially the Wittelsbach family, developed Bavarian cuisine and refined it to be presentable to the royal court. Since the 19th century, this cuisine has belonged to wealthy households, especially in cities.
The Munich Weißwurst was "invented" only in 1857. It is a reminder that some dishes now seen as ancient Bavarian tradition are surprisingly recent.
Knödel and noodles were a traditional festive dish in Bavaria. By the late 19th century, chopped pork with Knödel had become a typical Bavarian regional dish.

art.text: Karl Friedrich Schinkel was the most important architect of his style in Germany. In his most productive period he appealed to Greek rather than Roman architecture, avoiding the style linked to the recent French occupiers. His most famous buildings are found in and around Berlin.

The initial impetus for modernist architecture in Germany was mainly industrial construction, where design was not held back so much by prevailing historicism. Examples are the AEG Turbine Hall in Berlin by Peter Behrens (1908–1909) and the Fagus Factory by Walter Gropius in Alfeld an der Leine (1911–1914).

In 1905, a group of architecture students who wanted to be painters formed Die Brücke ("The Bridge") in Dresden. Its founders were Fritz Bleyl, Erich Heckel, Ernst Ludwig Kirchner and Karl Schmidt-Rottluff. It became one of two groups of German painters fundamental to expressionism.
In Berlin, Karl Friedrich Schinkel designed the Neue Wache (1816–1818) and the Altes Museum, or Old Museum, on Museum Island (1823–1830). Both are counted among his most famous buildings.
Gottfried Semper built the gallery (1855) at the Zwinger Palace and the Semperoper (1878) in Dresden. He was also involved with the first design of the Schwerin Palace.

Der Blaue Reiter ("The Blue Rider") formed in Munich in 1911. Wassily Kandinsky, Franz Marc, August Macke and others founded it after Kandinsky's painting Last Judgment was rejected from an exhibition by the Neue Künstlervereinigung, another artists' group he had belonged to.

Wilhelm II took an active interest in regulating art in Germany and criticized Impressionism as "gutter painting" (Gossenmalerei). In 1898 he forbade Käthe Kollwitz from being awarded a medal for her print series A Weavers' Revolt, shown in the Berlin Grand Exhibition of the Arts.
tags: Berlin Grand Exhibition of the Arts

art.text: Schinkel's Schauspielhaus (1819–1821) at the Gendarmenmarkt in Berlin replaced an earlier theatre that was destroyed by fire in 1817. It was built within a few years of that loss.

Gottfried Semper's buildings have features derived from the early Renaissance style and the Baroque. They even include Corinthian order pillars typical of ancient Greek architecture. This mixing of older styles is typical of historicism.
Die Brücke moved to Berlin in 1911 and dissolved in 1913. Perhaps the group's most important contribution was the rediscovery of the woodcut as a valid medium for original artistic expression.

In his 1892 book Degeneration, the critic Max Nordau attacked modern art as the work of people corrupted and enfeebled by modern life. He explained the painterliness of Impressionism as the sign of a diseased visual cortex. He drew on Cesare Lombroso's The Criminal Man of 1876.

The name Der Blaue Reiter came from Franz Marc's enthusiasm for horses and Wassily Kandinsky's love of blue. For Kandinsky, blue was the colour of spirituality, an idea in his 1911 book On the Spiritual in Art. He had also titled a painting Der Blaue Reiter in 1903.

war.text: In 1804, Napoleon declared the First French Empire. In response, Emperor Francis II of the Habsburg dynasty declared his personal domain the Austrian Empire and became Francis I of Austria. Two years later, in 1806, Napoleon forced the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire.
war.source_title: Flags of the Holy Roman Empire

war.text: The Austro-Prussian War was fought in 1866 between the Austrian Empire and the Kingdom of Prussia. It confirmed Prussia's superiority in military organization and technology over Austria at the time. The result was Prussian dominance over the German states.

The Holy Roman Empire ended on 6 August 1806, when Francis II abdicated his title and released all Imperial states and officials from their oaths and obligations. Before this, the empire had lacked both a central standing army and a central treasury.
war.source_title: Dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire

war.text: Austria fought Napoleon throughout the Napoleonic Wars, except between 1809 and 1813. In that period it was first allied with Napoleon during the invasion of Russia, then neutral during the first weeks of the Sixth Coalition War. Austria and its allies emerged victorious, leading to the Congress of Vienna.

The Austro-Prussian War grew out of a dispute over Schleswig-Holstein, which Prussia and Austria had conquered from Denmark and agreed to jointly occupy after the Second Schleswig War in 1864. The crisis began on 26 January 1866, when Prussia protested an Austrian decision in Holstein as a breach of joint sovereignty.

The Austro-Prussian War ended the German Confederation. The northern German states were united in the North German Confederation, which excluded Austria and the other southern German states. Italy also annexed the Austrian realm of Venetia, because Prussia had allied with the Kingdom of Italy.

Despite defeats at Marengo, Ulm, Austerlitz and Wagram, and territory lost in treaties such as Pressburg in 1806 and Schönbrunn in 1809, Austria played a decisive part in overthrowing Napoleon in the campaigns of 1813 to 1814. It joined a second invasion of France in 1815.
In March 1866, Austria reinforced its troops along its frontier with Prussia. Prussia responded on 28 March with a partial mobilization of five divisions.

Before 1866, Prussia and Austria had nearly gone to war in 1850 over Berlin's leadership of the Erfurt Union. Prussia backed down at that time. It had been contesting Austria's supremacy in Germany since at least then.

Russia was unlikely to side with Vienna in 1866 because of ill will over Francis Joseph's support for the Anglo-French alliance during the Crimean War. Russia had aided him against the Hungarian Revolution of 1848 to 1849. Prussia, by contrast, had signed the Alvensleben Convention with Russia in February 1863.

literature.text: The Brothers Grimm saw folk stories as a pure form of national literature and culture, a view that grew from the rise of Romanticism. They set out a method for collecting and recording tales that became the basis for folklore studies.
The physician Heinrich Hoffmann wrote Der Struwwelpeter, a book of cautionary tales, and published it in 1845. It was first given as a Christmas gift to his 3-year-old son.

Modern German science fiction was born in 1871 with the first short stories of Kurd Laßwitz and Albert Daiber. This was just as Jules Verne was reaching the peak of his output in France. The industrial revolutions and the rise of technology helped the genre take off.
The Grimms' first collection of tales was revised and republished many times between 1812 and 1857. Over those years it grew from 86 stories to more than 200.

Max and Moritz was written and illustrated by the poet and artist Wilhelm Busch and published in 1865. Inspired by Der Struwwelpeter, it became popular thanks to its goofy cartoon style and its rhymes.

Kurd Laßwitz's Auf zwei Planeten (1897) runs to almost a thousand pages. German explorers on a balloon trip to the North Pole discover a secret Martian station, and an incident threatens to lead to war. It sold 70,000 copies before the Third Reich banned it.

Bernhard Kellermann's Der Tunnel appeared in 1913 and was such a bestseller that it was adapted twice for the cinema within twenty years. The realist novel describes the economic and social consequences of building a gigantic rail tunnel under the Atlantic Ocean between Europe and America.

In 1838 the Brothers Grimm began writing a definitive German dictionary, the Deutsches Wörterbuch. They were never able to finish it. They also wrote collections of Germanic and Scandinavian mythologies.
Heinrich Hoffmann reillustrated Der Struwwelpeter himself in 1864. The book was still regarded as a classic, and the anniversary of the book and its legacy continued to be marked.
Carl Grunert published some thirty science fiction stories between 1904 and 1914. His most notable collections were Feinde im Weltall? (1907) and Der Marsspion (1908).

Besides writing fiction, Kurd Laßwitz was a publisher, mathematician and philosopher. His technical, philosophical and mathematical narratives were largely inspired by neo-Kantianism and by the work of the psycho-physicist Gustav Fechner.
Carl Grunert made numerous references to Jules Verne, Kurd Laßwitz and Herbert George Wells in his stories. He developed some of their ideas in original ways.

science.text: Before World War II, Germany had produced more Nobel laureates in scientific fields than any other nation. From the late 19th century, German was also one of the leading languages of science, alongside English and French.

The Industrial Revolution modernized the German economy and brought urban growth. During this period German universities became world-class centers for science. The first unification of Germany came in 1871 under Otto von Bismarck.
In 1895 Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen discovered X-rays. The achievement made him the first winner of the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901. It also eventually earned him an element name, roentgenium.
Heinrich Rudolf Hertz (1857–1894) did work on electromagnetic radiation that was pivotal to the development of modern telecommunication. The unit of frequency, the hertz, was named in his honor.

Joseph von Fraunhofer (1787–1826) discovered the Fraunhofer lines in spectroscopy. He is named among the key German physicists who came before Einstein and Planck, together with Hermann von Helmholtz (1821–1894).

By 1854 Prévinaire had modified a Perrotine, the mechanical block-printing machine invented in 1834 by Louis-Jérôme Perrot. Instead of printing, it applied a resin to both sides of the cloth. This mechanically applied resin took the place of the wax in the batik process.

politics.text: In 1806 the last Holy Roman Emperor, Francis II of the House of Habsburg-Lorraine, abdicated on the 6th of August and released all Imperial states and officials from their oaths. It ended an institution that had claimed to continue the ancient Roman Empire since the Middle Ages.
politics.source_title: Dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire

politics.text: On 18 January 1871, the south German states joined the North German Confederation, and the German Empire was founded. Wilhelm I, King of Prussia from the House of Hohenzollern, took the title of German Emperor. Otto von Bismarck became chancellor, the head of government.

The German Empire consisted of 25 states, each with its own nobility, including four kingdoms, six grand duchies and three free Hanseatic cities. Prussia was only one of the four kingdoms, yet it held about two-thirds of the Empire's population and territory. Its dominance was written into the constitution because the king of Prussia was also the German Emperor.

In 1806 Francis II abdicated as the last Holy Roman Emperor and released all imperial states and officials from their oaths. Earlier abdications had returned the crown to the electors so they could choose a new emperor. Francis II's abdication dissolved the empire itself, so there were no more electors.
politics.source_title: Dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire

politics.text: In 1804, Napoleon declared the First French Empire, and Francis II responded by declaring his personal domain the Austrian Empire. He became Francis I of Austria while still Holy Roman Emperor. The empire's flag took the black and gold of the old imperial banner, and those colours continued as the Habsburg flag until 1918.
politics.source_title: Flags of the Holy Roman Empire

politics.text: Bismarck served as the first and longest-tenured chancellor of the German Empire, from 1871 to 1890. His tenure began with liberal measures but shifted toward conservatism, marked by the Kulturkampf against the Catholic Church. In 1879 he concluded the Dual Alliance with Austria-Hungary, which grew into the Triple Alliance with Italy in 1882.

After Austria was defeated in the Austro-Prussian War of 1866 and the German Confederation was dissolved, the Austro-Hungarian Compromise of 1867 was adopted. It joined the Kingdom of Hungary and the Empire of Austria on an equal basis as the Dual Monarchy of Austria-Hungary.

The Holy Roman Empire was dissolved on 6 August 1806, when Francis II abdicated after military defeat by Napoleon at the Battle of Austerlitz in 1805. Napoleon reorganized much of the empire into the Confederation of the Rhine, a French satellite.

The Prince-Electors, who had elected the Holy Roman Emperor, were abolished in 1806. In 1803 Napoleon's changes had created new electors for Württemberg, Baden, Hesse-Kassel and Salzburg, but none of them ever cast a vote.

Napoleon's aggression reshaped the electors of the Holy Roman Empire. In 1803 new electoral posts were created for Württemberg, Baden, Hesse-Kassel and Salzburg, bringing the total to ten. None of the new electors ever cast a vote, because the empire was abolished in 1806 and the posts were never confirmed by the Emperor.

After the empire's abolition in 1806, the Electors of Bavaria, Württemberg and Saxony styled themselves Kings. The Electors of Baden, Regensburg and Würzburg became Grand Dukes. The Elector of Hesse-Kassel kept the meaningless title Elector of Hesse, but Napoleon soon exiled him and annexed Kassel to the new Kingdom of Westphalia.

The Hohenzollerns were uneasy about an imperial title even after 1871, since they lacked imperial ancestry. When Frederick III reigned in 1888, he was numbered after the earlier king Frederick II, not after the medieval Emperor Frederick III. This kept the new empire's numbering tied to the Kings of Prussia.
politics.source_title: Dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire

politics.text: The black-white-red flag began as the national flag of the North German Confederation, which Prussia formed in 1866. Wilhelm I liked it partly because the absence of gold showed the new state excluded the black and gold Austrian Empire. It was only officially adopted as the German Empire's national flag in 1892, under Wilhelm II.

Bismarck was annoyed by military interference in foreign policy. In 1887, the army tried to convince the emperor to declare war on Russia and encouraged Austria-Hungary to attack Russia. Bismarck never controlled the army but complained vehemently, and the military leaders drew back.

In the July Crisis of 1914, chief of staff Helmuth von Moltke advised his Austro-Hungarian counterpart to mobilise against Russia at once, without telling the emperor or chancellor. Historian Gordon A. Craig says the crucial decisions of 1914 were made by soldiers who showed almost complete disregard for political considerations.

philosophy.text: German idealism grew out of the work of Immanuel Kant and became one of the most intellectually fertile movements in modern philosophy. Its leading figures were Kant, Fichte, Schelling and Hegel. Some compare its prominence to the golden age of philosophy in ancient Athens.

In the 1850s the materialism controversy challenged conventions in German thought. Zoologist Carl Vogt argued mental processes were entirely physical, stating that thoughts stand in the same relation to the brain as bile does to the liver or urine to the kidneys.

Austrian physicist Ernst Mach propounded neutral monism in works such as Analysis of Sensations (1885). He held that everything was physical, but equally a complex of sensations, rejecting an external world independent of consciousness.

German idealism effectively ended with Hegel's death in 1831, but its influence was immense. Hegel's system was widely seen as the culmination of the movement, and much of 19th-century philosophy was defined by reactions to it.

Joseph Dietzgen (1828-1888) independently reached conclusions very close to those of Marx and Engels. Working in a tannery in St. Petersburg, he devoted all his leisure time to philosophy, political economy and socialism.

Wilhelm Dilthey (1833-1911), along with Nietzsche, Georg Simmel and Ludwig Klages, founded the intuitionist and irrationalist school of German Lebensphilosophie. Dilthey was a historist who initiated a Romantic renaissance with his Schleiermacher biography and works on Novalis and Hölderlin.

The collapse of idealism gave rise to two main streams of thought: philosophies of praxis focused on political and social transformation, and philosophies of science aligned with positivism and the empirical sciences. Paradoxically, both were fed by ideas that had grown in the lap of idealism.
In the materialism controversy, Carl Vogt was supported by Ludwig Büchner (1824-1899). He was opposed by Rudolf Wagner (1805-1864) and Justus von Liebig (1803-1873).

Ernst Mach and his teacher Gustav Kirchoff believed in the economy of thought, meant to eliminate all superfluous metaphysical elements. Mach's rival was Ludwig Boltzmann, notable for the Boltzmann brain thought experiment.

In 1877 Ernst Kapp wrote "Grundlinien einer Philosophie der Technik" (Elements of a Philosophy of Technology). It identifies tools and weapons as different forms of 'organ projections'. It also analyses language and the state as extensions of mental life, long before Marshall McLuhan popularised such ideas.

Hegel claimed that the history of philosophy had reached its end with his system. This was often read as saying all philosophical possibility was exhausted. It can also be understood as saying philosophy had completed a historical cycle by overcoming the subject-object dualism that structured modern thought.

Joseph Dietzgen wrote a large philosophical treatise, The Essence of the Mental Labor of Man (1869), a review of the first volume of Das Kapital. After returning to Germany, he moved again to America, where he wrote Excursions of a Socialist in the Field of the Theory of Knowledge (1887).
tags: The Essence of the Mental Labor of Man

philosophy.text: Ernst Kapp, a philosopher of technology and geographer born in 1808, was prosecuted for sedition after publishing a small article in 1849. He was forced to leave Germany and emigrated to central Texas, where he worked as a farmer, geographer and inventor.

culture.text: In 1800, Germany was overwhelmingly rural: only 10% of people lived in communities of 5,000 or more, and only 2% lived in cities of more than 100,000. After 1815, young people from the countryside poured into towns and the urban population grew.

Physical culture, a health and strength movement, originated in the 19th century in Germany, the UK and the US. After 1848, German immigrants to the United States introduced a gymnastics-based system that became popular, especially in colleges.

In the 19th century, biblical scholarship, progress in natural science and criticism of oppressive social conditions led many Germans to reject traditional theology. By 1859 some had founded the Union of Free Religious Communities of Germany, for people who consider themselves religious without belonging to an established church.

In 19th-century Europe the Catholic Church strongly opposed liberalism, and culture wars were launched in Germany, Italy, Belgium and France. The Church strongly emphasized personal piety, even as people in Europe generally moved away from religious observance and toward secularism.
Berlin grew from 172,000 inhabitants in 1800 to 826,000 in 1870. Munich grew over the same period from 40,000 to 269,000, showing how quickly German city life was changing.

German nationalism grew in the 19th century as the Holy Roman Empire dissolved, and discussions of German identity centered on a common language, culture, descent and history. German is still widely seen as a necessary criterion for German national belonging.

During the 19th century, many Germans emigrated to the New World, especially the United States. Large numbers also went to Canada and Brazil, and they founded sizable communities in New Zealand and Australia.

Bismarck's Kulturkampf against the Catholic Church in Germany brought heavy penalties and imprisonments, and by 1878 only three of eight Prussian dioceses still had bishops, some 1,125 of 4,600 parishes were vacant, and nearly 1,800 priests had ended up in jail or in exile. Catholic newspapers were confiscated, associations dissolved and civil servants dismissed. The Church denounced the harsh laws as anti-catholic, and in the following elections the Center Party won a quarter of the seats in the Imperial Diet.

In the United States, local Turner clubs introduced 'German gymnastics' as physical education into colleges and public schools. Because Turner was seen as 'non-American', the German system never became the dominant form.
In 1881 in Frankfurt am Main, Ludwig Büchner established the German Freethinkers League, the first German organisation for atheists and agnostics. The Deutscher Monistenbund followed in 1906.
